title: Poverty breeds violence
hookLine: a king neglects the poor; theft, then weapons, then killing follow
last: COME BACK TO YOUR OWN GROUND.

cards: In the old story there are wheel-turning kings, rulers so just that a great jeweled wheel appears in the sky and rolls ahead of them, and other kingdoms simply welcome them.
The first, Dalhanemi, grows old, hands the throne to his son, and goes forth. The wheel vanishes. The son asks his father what to do, and is told: the wheel isn't an inheritance.
You have to earn it. Rule by the Dhamma. Protect everyone, even the birds and beasts.
And give wealth to those who have none. Generations later, a king forgets that last part.

teach.h: HE DIDN'T GIVE TO THE NEEDY.
teach.b: This king, in the Cakkavatti Sihanada, rules by his own ideas. He protects people, but he doesn't give wealth to the needy. And so, the text says, poverty spreads.
Then a man steals. He's caught and brought before the king. Why did you steal?
Because I had nothing to live on, sire. So the king gives him money: live on this, support your parents, your wife and children, start a business, give to holy people. Good.
But word gets around, and others steal, hoping for the same. Now the king panics. If I keep giving money to thieves, theft will only grow.
So he does the opposite: he has the next thief bound, paraded through the streets to the beat of a harsh drum, and beheaded.
People hear, and think: then we'll carry sharp swords, and kill those we rob so nobody can report us. Theft becomes killing. Then lying, to cover it.
Then slander, and on down a long list, and with every step, human life gets shorter and uglier. Look at the chain the sutta draws. The trouble doesn't start with a wicked thief.
It starts with a king who didn't share. Then a harsh answer to a symptom makes it worse. It's an old Indian story, and the Buddha tells it as a story, with fantastic numbers and ages.
But the chain it draws doesn't need the fantastic numbers: when people have nothing, and the only answer is punishment, the text says violence grows.

how: Buddhist social thinkers in Asia and beyond often cite the Cakkavatti Sihanada Sutta when they speak about poverty and crime, and many Buddhist communities run food banks, clinics and relief work.

o: poverty, having nothing to live on
a harsh drum beaten for the guilty

games.q: poverty breeds violence: tap the pairs.

s: in DN 26 the trouble begins with a wicked thief
it begins with a king who stops giving wealth to the needy.
the king first responds to theft by giving the thief money
then others steal hoping for the same, and he turns to execution.
the harsh punishment ends the crime wave
thieves arm themselves and begin killing those they rob.

games.q: you're the king. a thief says he stole because he had nothing to live on. what does the king in the story do first?
o: give him money to live on and support his family.
games.why: he gives him money. only when others copy the thief does he turn to execution, and the violence grows.

practice: Think of someone who doesn't have enough, a person you pass on the street, a family you've heard about, and let their situation be real for a moment, not an idea.
Breathe with it, then let one small, concrete thing come to mind that you could give: money, food, time, a phone call. You don't have to decide yet; just let it be clear.

wordCard.voice: Daliddiya. In DN 26 a king stops giving to the needy; theft follows, then a harsh punishment, then weapons and killing. Today's word.

orig.note: Pali daliddiya: poverty. in DN 26 it spreads when the king stops giving to those without wealth.

carryVoice: Your line: give something real, however small. The trouble began with a king who didn't share. See you tomorrow.

sources.ref: Digha Nikaya 26 (Cakkavatti Sihanada Sutta), the wheel-turning kings and the spread of poverty
